title: Dal Makhani
description: Whole black urad dal and rajma, soaked overnight and simmered for over an hour until velvety, then finished with butter and cream — the dish that defines a Punjabi dhaba menu.

ingredients.item: urad dal (whole black gram), soaked overnight

steps: Drain the soaked urad dal and rajma, rinse, then pressure cook with 6 cups water and salt for 8-10 whistles until completely soft and mashable.
Once the pressure releases, mash some of the dal against the side of the pot to thicken the base, keeping the rest whole.
Heat butter in a heavy pan, add the ginger-garlic paste and cook until the raw smell disappears.
Off the heat, stir in red chilli powder and turmeric with a splash of water so the powdered spices bloom without scorching.
Return to low heat, add the tomato puree, and simmer until the fat separates at the edges.
Pour the cooked dal into the tomato masala, add garam masala, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 45-60 minutes, stirring occasionally so it does not catch at the bottom.
Stir in the fresh cream and remaining butter, then simmer 5 more minutes.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms and scatter over the top before serving with rice or naan.
tips: Soaking the dal and rajma overnight is what gives dal makhani its silky texture — do not skip it.
The dish improves overnight in the fridge; reheat gently with a splash of milk or water.
nutritionNote: Urad dal and rajma with rice form a complete plant protein; the butter and cream load is generous here, so keep the kids' butter swirl light and serve alongside a cucumber salad.

title: Malai Kofta
description: Golden fried potato-paneer dumplings bathed in a cashew-tomato gravy finished with cream — heavily spiced and rich rather than chilli-hot, a classic dinner-party centrepiece.

ingredients.item: cashews, soaked and ground to a paste

steps: Mix the mashed potato, paneer, cornflour, chilli powder and salt, and shape into 8 small balls.
Heat oil to medium and deep fry the koftas in batches until golden brown; drain on paper towels.
Heat ghee in a pan and add the cumin seeds, letting them sizzle.
Add the ginger-garlic paste and sauté until the raw smell goes.
Off the heat, stir in the kashmiri chilli powder and garam masala with a splash of water so they don't scorch.
Return to heat, pour in the tomato puree and cashew paste, and simmer 12-15 minutes until the gravy thickens and the oil separates.
Stir in the cream and a pinch of sugar, then simmer 2 minutes more.
Just before serving, gently lower the koftas into the warm gravy so they don't turn soggy.
tips: Add the koftas to the gravy only right before serving — sitting in liquid too long makes them fall apart.
Squeeze the mashed potato mixture dry so the koftas hold together while frying.
nutritionNote: Deep-fried koftas in a cashew-cream gravy make this an occasional treat rather than a weeknight staple; balance the meal with a simple salad and keep the kids' portion smaller and less cream-heavy.

title: Kadai Paneer
description: Paneer and peppers tossed through a coarsely crushed coriander-cumin-black pepper masala with a quick tomato base — a dry kadai dish with a real spicy-hot kick, not a creamy gravy.
steps: Dry roast the coriander seeds, cumin seeds, dried red chillies and black peppercorns until fragrant, then coarsely crush them in a mortar.
Heat oil in a kadai (or wok) and add half of the crushed spice mix, letting it sizzle for a few seconds.
Add the cubed onion and capsicum and stir-fry on high heat for 3-4 minutes so they stay crunchy.
Push the vegetables aside, add the ginger-garlic paste to the empty space, and cook until the raw smell disappears.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook until they soften and the oil starts to separate.
Off the heat, stir in turmeric, kashmiri chilli powder and salt with a splash of water so the powdered spices don't burn.
Return to heat, add the paneer cubes and remaining crushed spice mix, and toss gently for 2-3 minutes until everything is coated.
Finish with kasuri methi and fresh coriander, and serve immediately while the paneer is soft.
tips: Keep the paneer cubes large so they don't break up while tossing.
Do not overcook the capsicum and onion — kadai paneer should stay a little crunchy, not stewed.
kidNote: For the kids' bowls, spoon out paneer and vegetables before adding the dried red chilli and kashmiri chilli powder to the rest, and finish their portion with a small swirl of cream to cool it down while keeping the roasted whole-spice aroma.
nutritionNote: Paneer supplies protein and calcium; this is a fairly dry, oil-light dish once the frying is done, so pair it with a dal or rice for a balanced plate.

title: Bhindi Masala
description: Okra fried first until the sliminess disappears, then tossed through a quick onion-tomato masala — an everyday Punjabi side, warmly spiced rather than hot, ready in well under 40 minutes.

ingredients.item: okra (bhindi), washed, dried and cut into 1-inch pieces

steps: Wash and completely dry the okra before chopping — leftover moisture is what makes it slimy.
Heat half the oil in a wide pan and shallow-fry the okra for 6-8 minutes over medium heat until it's no longer sticky; set it aside.
In the same pan, heat the remaining oil and add the cumin seeds until they sizzle.
Add the chopped onion and cook until golden, then stir in the ginger-garlic paste until fragrant.
Add the chopped tomatoes and salt, and cook until soft and the oil separates.
Off the heat, stir in turmeric, red chilli powder and coriander powder with a splash of water so they bloom without burning.
Return the pan to heat, fold in the fried okra and garam masala, and cook uncovered for 3-4 minutes so it stays semi-dry.
Scatter fresh coriander over the top and serve with roti or dal-rice.
tips: Frying the okra separately first is the one step that stops bhindi masala turning slimy.
Keep the pan uncovered once the okra goes back in — trapped steam brings the sliminess back.
nutritionNote: Okra brings fibre and folate; pair with a dal and rice or roti for a balanced plate — this dish is naturally light on dairy, so it works well alongside a richer paneer curry.

title: Sarson ka Saag
description: Mustard greens simmered with spinach and radish until soft, coarsely pureed, then finished with a ghee-garlic tempering — earthy and warmly spiced, the classic partner for makki roti.

ingredients.item: mustard greens (sarson), washed and roughly chopped
spinach and bathua leaves (or extra spinach), washed and roughly chopped

steps: Pressure cook the mustard greens, spinach, radish, onion, garlic, ginger, green chilli and tomato together with a cup of water for 4-5 whistles until completely soft.
Once cool, blend the mixture coarsely — sarson ka saag should keep some texture, not be a smooth puree.
Transfer to a heavy pot, whisk in the maize flour, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 20-25 minutes, stirring often so it doesn't stick.
Adjust the salt and add a little water if the saag gets too thick.
For the tempering, heat ghee in a small pan and add the dried red chillies and asafoetida.
Add the sliced garlic and fry until golden, then pour the sizzling tempering straight over the saag.
Stir half the tempering through and keep the rest for spooning on top at the table.
Serve hot with makki roti, a cube of butter and a little jaggery on the side.
tips: Making the saag a day ahead and reheating it actually deepens the flavour.
Keep some texture when blending — an overly smooth saag loses its traditional bite.
nutritionNote: A very high-iron, high-fibre green vegetable dish; the ghee tempering is part of the traditional flavour, so keep the kids' butter garnish modest and serve with makki roti and a bowl of yoghurt.

title: Chicken 65
description: Bite-sized chicken marinated in yoghurt, ginger-garlic and chilli, deep fried till crisp, then tossed with curry leaves and green chilli — properly spicy-hot, a South Indian restaurant favourite.

ingredients.item: boneless chicken, cut into bite-sized pieces

steps: Whisk together yoghurt, ginger-garlic paste, chilli powder, turmeric and salt, then marinate the chicken in it for at least 30 minutes (longer in the fridge is better).
Just before frying, dust the marinated chicken with rice flour and cornflour so it turns crisp.
Heat oil for deep frying to medium-hot and fry the chicken in small batches for 5-6 minutes until golden and cooked through; drain on paper towels.
In a separate pan, heat the tempering oil and add the mustard seeds until they crackle.
Add the curry leaves and slit green chillies and fry for a few seconds until the leaves turn crisp.
Add the chopped garlic and cook until golden.
Off the heat, stir in the extra red chilli powder so it colours the oil without burning.
Toss the fried chicken through the tempering over high heat for a minute so every piece is coated, then serve immediately.
tips: A quick second fry after a short rest gives the extra crunch restaurants get.
Marinating overnight in the fridge makes the chicken noticeably more tender.
kidNote: Fry the kids' portion of chicken from the same yoghurt marinade, then toss it through only the crackled mustard seeds, curry leaves and garlic — no slit green chillies and no extra chilli powder — so it stays crunchy and fragrant without the heat.
nutritionNote: A good source of protein, but it is deep-fried, so serve it as a starter alongside a vegetable-forward main rather than the whole meal, and keep the kids' portion to a smaller handful.

title: Goan Fish Curry
description: Firm fish simmered in a ground coconut, red chilli and kokum gravy — tangy and coconut-rich rather than tomato-sweet, with a sour edge from kokum that marks it out as distinctly Goan.

ingredients.item: firm white fish (kingfish or pomfret), cut into steaks

ingredients.note: or 1 tbsp tamarind pulp — kokum gives the authentic sour note

steps: Rub the fish pieces with turmeric and lime juice and set aside to marinate while you make the masala.
Grind the grated coconut, dried kashmiri chillies, cumin seeds, coriander seeds, garlic and the roughly chopped onion with a little water into a smooth paste.
Heat coconut oil in a clay pot or heavy pan and add the sliced onion, cooking until soft and lightly golden.
Add the ground coconut-spice paste and cook on low heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until the raw smell disappears and the oil begins to separate.
Pour in 1.5 cups of water, add the kokum and salt, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Slide in the marinated fish and slit green chillies, cover, and simmer for 8-10 minutes without stirring hard so the fish stays intact.
Taste and adjust the sourness with more kokum water if needed — the curry should be tangy, not sweet.
Rest for a few minutes off the heat before serving with steamed rice.
tips: Do not boil the curry hard once the fish goes in — a gentle simmer keeps it from breaking apart.
Kokum is worth sourcing for real Goan sourness; tamarind gives a different, sharper tang.
kidNote: Ladle out the kids' fish and a little gravy before adding the slit green chillies, and leave a spoonful of the ground paste's dried chillies out of their portion so it stays mild while keeping the coconut and kokum flavour.
nutritionNote: Fish and coconut provide protein and healthy fats; this curry is coconut-oil based rather than cream-based, so it pairs well with plain rice and a simple cucumber salad.

title: Kerala Avial
description: Mixed vegetables simmered until just tender, then folded through a coarse coconut-yoghurt paste and finished with raw coconut oil and curry leaves — mild and mellow, a Kerala sadya staple.
steps: Put the carrot, drumstick, raw banana, pumpkin, potato and beans into a pot with turmeric, salt and just enough water to cover, and simmer covered for 12-15 minutes until tender but not mushy.
While the vegetables cook, coarsely grind the coconut, cumin seeds and green chillies with a splash of water — keep it grainy, not a smooth paste.
Once the vegetables are tender and most of the water has cooked off, stir in the coconut paste and simmer for 2-3 minutes.
Take the pot off the heat and fold in the whisked yoghurt so it doesn't split.
Drizzle raw coconut oil over the top and scatter curry leaves without cooking them further, then cover for a couple of minutes so the aroma settles in.
Serve warm alongside rice as part of a Kerala meal.
tips: Cut every vegetable to a similar baton shape so they all cook evenly in the same time.
Add the yoghurt off the heat — boiling it after that point will curdle the avial.
nutritionNote: A vegetable-forward dish with coconut and yoghurt rather than any added cream or ghee; a good way to get several vegetables into one bowl, and it pairs naturally with a protein-rich dal or fish curry.

title: Sambar
description: Toor dal simmered with mixed vegetables, tamarind and a roasted spice powder, finished with a mustard-curry leaf tempering — a tangy, everyday South Indian stew, warmly spiced, not fiery.

ingredients.item: tamarind pulp, soaked in warm water

steps: Pressure cook the toor dal with turmeric and a cup of water for 3-4 whistles until soft, then mash it lightly.
In a separate pot, simmer the drumstick, carrot, pumpkin, onion and tomato with the tamarind water and a little salt until the vegetables are just tender.
Stir in the sambar powder and the cooked dal, then simmer for 6-8 minutes so the flavours come together.
Adjust the consistency with water and check the salt and tang, adding more tamarind water if needed.
For the tempering, heat oil or ghee in a small pan and add the mustard seeds until they pop.
Add the cumin seeds, dried red chillies, asafoetida and curry leaves, and let them sizzle for a few seconds.
Pour the sizzling tempering straight over the sambar and stir through.
Serve hot with steamed rice, idli or dosa.
tips: Add the sambar powder to the vegetables, not the dal, so its flavour doesn't get lost in the mash.
Simmer gently once the dal goes in — a hard boil can make the sambar taste flat.
nutritionNote: Toor dal with rice forms a complete protein, and the mixed vegetables add fibre; this is a naturally light dish that pairs well with a richer paneer or kofta curry on the same table.

title: Rasam
description: A thin, peppery tomato-tamarind broth tempered with mustard seeds and curry leaves — sipped as a soup or spooned over rice, warmly spiced with black pepper rather than chilli-hot.

ingredients.item: tamarind pulp, soaked in warm water

steps: Pressure cook the toor dal with turmeric and a cup of water for 3-4 whistles until soft, then mash it well.
In a pot, combine the tamarind water, chopped tomatoes and 2 cups of water, and simmer for 10 minutes until the tomatoes soften.
Stir in the rasam powder, salt and jaggery, and simmer for 3-4 minutes.
Add the mashed dal and enough water to thin the rasam to a soupy consistency, then bring it just to a simmer — do not let it boil hard once the dal is in.
For the tempering, heat ghee in a small pan and add the mustard seeds until they crackle.
Add the cumin seeds, dried red chillies, asafoetida and curry leaves, and let them sizzle for a few seconds.
Pour the tempering over the rasam and scatter fresh coriander on top before serving.
Serve hot as a soup on its own, or spoon over steamed rice.
tips: Never let rasam boil hard once the dal is added — it turns cloudy and loses its light texture.
A ripe, well-crushed tomato makes a real difference to the final tang.
nutritionNote: Light on the stomach and mildly protein-rich from the toor dal; a good way to add pepper and tamarind's digestive qualities to a meal without extra fat, and easy to make milder for kids by using less pepper in the rasam powder.
